    Criticality-aware Monitoring and Orchestration for Containerized Industry 4.0 Environments

    Marco Barletta, Marcello Cinque, Luigi De Simone and Raffaele Della Corte

    Abstract

    The evolution of industrial environments makes the reconfigurability and flexibility key requirements to rapidly adapt to changeable market needs. Computing paradigms like Edge/Fog computing are able to provide the required flexibility and scalability while guaranteeing low latencies and response times. Orchestration systems play a key role in these environments, enforcing automatic management of resources and workloads’ lifecycle, and drastically reducing the need for manual interventions. However, they do not currently meet industrial non-functional requirements, such as real-timeliness, determinism, reliability, and support for mixed-criticality workloads.

    In this article, we present k4.0s, an orchestration system for Industry 4.0 (I4.0) environments, which enables the support for real-time and mixed-criticality workloads. We highlight through experiments the need for novel monitoring approaches and propose a workflow for selecting monitoring metrics, which depends on both workload requirements and hosting node guarantees. We introduce new abstractions for the components of a cluster in order to enable criticality-aware monitoring and orchestration of real-time industrial workloads. Finally, we design an orchestration system architecture that reflects the proposed model, introducing new components and prototyping a Kubernetes-based implementation, taking the first steps towards a fully I4.0-enabled orchestration system.

1 INTRODUCTION
The vision of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) foresees the automatic and continuous reconfiguration of factory
floors and production lines to adapt to evolving business goals. This includes the automatic re-
arrangement of the production lines through collaborative robots, as well as the continuous recon-
figuration, deployment, and monitoring of new industrial components [1, 2].
The manifold I4.0 use-case scenarios can include highly available distributed control systems [3],
populated by virtualized Programmable Logic Controller (PLCs) [4], wireless connected heteroge-
neous things (i.e., the Industrial Internet of Things paradigm) [5], online predictive maintenance,
digital twin-based production processes [6], and so forth. To support these use cases, more and
more industrial environments leverage Fog/Edge computing paradigms to offload the high compu-
tational costs of, for example, Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning algorithms from devices
and robots to nearly located micro datacenters, better equipped in terms of resources [7, 8]. Fur-
thermore, replacing traditional machinery with softwarized industrial elements, according to the
Software Defined Anything trend, allows easier management, reconfiguration, and replacement of
the components, avoiding frequent manual intervention.
However, the paradigm shift requires consolidating heterogeneous services on the same edge
node, e.g., real-time control, machine learning algorithms, and high-speed data acquisition, each
of them with different requirements [9]. Hence, the concepts of Fog/Edge computing and mixed-
criticality systems become strictly intertwined, and the whole factory floor can be seen as a mixed-
criticality system, with each node running jobs with different levels of criticality, i.e., the designa-
tion of the level of assurance against failure needed for a system component [10].
Virtualization is seen as an enabling technology for the implementation of mixed-criticality com-
ponents since it provides support for resource abstraction, partitioning, and multiplexing, consoli-
dating multiple Operating Systems (OSs) on the same hardware [11, 12]. However, critical compo-
nents must often meet temporal requirements, and consolidating real-time and general-purpose
systems on the same System-on-a-Chip (SoC) requires ad hoc solutions [13]. One drawback of soft-
ware virtualization is the overhead that hinders the efficient usage of hardware resources. There-
fore, over time several proposals have risen to mitigate the overhead, such as hardware-assisted
virtualization or para-virtualization. In this perspective, lightweight virtualization technologies
(e.g., containers) are gaining the limelight in industrial environments as a way to pack and deploy
low-latency and bandwidth-efficient services with reduced overhead and higher scalability com-
pared to classical hypervisor-based solutions [14–16]. Nevertheless, OS-level virtualization (i.e.,
containers) is known to suffer from a reduced degree of isolation compared to hypervisor-based
virtualization; thus, it cannot be seen as a panacea [17]. Containers are also seamlessly integrated
into orchestration systems (e.g., Docker Swarm [18], Kubernetes [19], Apache Mesos [20]), which
foster fully automated management. Orchestration systems are distributed systems that provide
the automatic placement, deployment, monitoring, and migration of the packaged software across
the infrastructure, behaving as cloud operating systems that manage hardware resources while ab-
stracting their use [21, 22]. They represent a valuable technology to manage softwarized industrial
components and to allow the required flexibility and intent-driven reconfiguration.
Currently, available orchestration systems are designed and tailored to cloud requirements. De-
spite the efforts, support for hard real-time applications with different levels of criticality and
nodes with uneven and limited computing resources, special devices, and different isolation guar-
antees is not mature yet [7, 23]. As a consequence, several studies investigated the feasibility of an
orchestration-powered real-time cloud, integrating the support for real-time and high-availability
services into Kubernetes [3, 24–28], the most widely adopted framework for managing contain-
ers, characterized by a rich feature set. Despite the existing solutions introducing the support
for deploying real-time containers, criticality-aware orchestration is still at the dawn. Specifically,

Criticality-aware Monitoring and Orchestration 5:3
current solutions lack determinism (e.g., time-bounded placement and migration of resources),
support for heterogeneous platforms and devices (in terms of OS/hypervisor), and capability of ad-
dressing the different degrees of isolation required by real-time workloads [29, 30]. Furthermore,
the heterogeneity of platforms, which feature Multiprocessor System-on-Chip (MPSoC), FPGAs,
GPUs, and various I/O devices, leads to the need for solutions that integrate hybrid virtualization
technologies, like hypervisor-based containers [31, 32].
To overcome current limitations, in this article we propose a criticality-aware orchestration so-
lution for I4.0. In particular, we propose a model and an architecture enabling software placement,
monitoring, and migration policies based on the criticality of the software component to be de-
ployed. The objective is to guarantee the isolation of high-critical workloads while not impacting
the performance of the less critical ones. The policies are based on the characteristics of nodes such
as the isolation and timeliness provided by the hardware/software of the nodes, required network
capabilities, and available resources.
In detail, our contributions are:
• Introducing a model for criticality-aware monitoring and orchestration of I4.0 workloads,
taking into account (1) the real-time assurance to be provided by the resources of the node,
(2) the criticality and real-time requirements of the workloads, and (3) the topology of the
Fog/Edge infrastructure.
• Designing and prototyping an orchestration system architecture, namely K4.0s, which com-
plies with the proposed model, by adding new components that handle the extended abstrac-
tions. Our proposal is based on Kubernetes and it is publicly available. The architecture is
designed to be open to different virtualization approaches, like OS-level virtualization and
hypervisor-based containers, in order to meet diversified requirements.
• Performing an experimental analysis to understand the behavior of real-time critical work-
loads running on top of variously configured nodes with co-located stress loads. Relying on
the results, we propose a workflow to derive suitable metrics to build a monitor that depends
on both workload requirements and node guarantees.
The article extends our previous work [33], where we introduced K4.0s, by (1) extending the pre-
viously proposed model with novel abstractions, e.g., introducing individual assurance levels for
resources; (2) providing further experiments highlighting the need for novel monitoring strategies,
based on both workload and node characteristics, including a monitoring overhead analysis and a
schedulability comparison with a vanilla solution; and (3) proposing a workflow for selecting key
monitoring metrics, generalizing the approach to any task-level metric.
The rest of the article is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses related work, while Section 3
provides some basic knowledge and terminology of orchestration systems used in the article. Sec-
tion 4 schematizes the problem that prevents the use of orchestration in I4.0. Section 5 introduces
our system model and the proposed abstractions, while Section 6 describes the proposed architec-
ture and the details of our Kubernetes-based implementation. Section 7 presents our experimental
campaign as well as the proposed process to determine the most useful monitoring metrics. Finally,
Section 8 concludes the article.
2 RELATED WORK
Current orchestration systems, such as Docker Swarm [18], Kubernetes [19], and Apache Mesos
[20], and monitoring solutions, such as Kubernetes Metric server [34], Prometheus [35], Telegraf
[36], and Victoria metrics [37], are mainly designed for cloud environments, where the presence
of both resourceful nodes and workloads that do not require strict timing constraints can be
